title: Hydrogen — Chemistry and Uses
topicTitle: Hydrogen: chemistry of atomic and nascent hydrogen; isotopes of hydrogen and their uses; application of hydrogen as fuel; heavy water and its applications
notes: **Isotopes of Hydrogen:** Hydrogen has three naturally occurring isotopes: protium ($^1_1\text{H}$, ~99.985%), deuterium ($^2_1\text{H}$ or D, ~0.015%), and tritium ($^3_1\text{H}$, trace). Protium has only a proton and no neutron; deuterium has one neutron; tritium has two neutrons and is radioactive with a half-life of 12.3 years.

**Atomic Hydrogen:** Produced by passing molecular hydrogen ($H_2$) through an electric arc at ~3000°C, causing homolytic fission: $H_2 \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2H\cdot$. The bond dissociation energy is 436 kJ/mol. Atomic hydrogen is highly reactive and recombines exothermically on a cool surface, releasing intense heat used in atomic hydrogen welding.

**Nascent Hydrogen:** Hydrogen produced *in situ* during a chemical reaction, e.g., $Zn + 2HCl \rightarrow ZnCl_2 + [H]$. Nascent hydrogen is more reactive than ordinary $H_2$ because it is in a freshly generated, high-energy atomic state before recombination. It can reduce substances that molecular hydrogen cannot, such as converting $Fe_2O_3$ to $Fe$.

**Position in Periodic Table:** Hydrogen occupies a unique position — it resembles alkali metals (ns¹ configuration, +1 oxidation state) and halogens (needs one electron for duet, -1 in metal hydrides, diatomic gas). It is placed separately in most periodic tables.

**Preparation of Hydrogen:** Laboratory method: $Zn + H_2SO_4(dil) \rightarrow ZnSO_4 + H_2\uparrow$. Industrial method: steam passing over red-hot coke (water-gas: $C + H_2O \rightarrow CO + H_2$), followed by the water-gas shift reaction ($CO + H_2O \rightarrow CO_2 + H_2$). Electrolysis of acidified water also yields high-purity hydrogen.

**Properties of Hydrogen:** A colourless, odourless, tasteless gas. It is the lightest element (molar mass 2 g/mol). It is sparingly soluble in water. Chemically, it acts as a reducing agent: $CuO + H_2 \rightarrow Cu + H_2O$, and as an oxidising agent with active metals: $2Na + H_2 \rightarrow 2NaH$.

**Hydride Classification:** Ionic/saline hydrides (NaH, CaH₂ — metal + H⁻), covalent/molecular hydrides (CH₄, NH₃, H₂O — non-metal + H), and metallic/interstitial hydrides (TiH₂, LaH₃ — transition metal + H stored in lattice). Ionic hydrides conduct electricity when molten.

**Heavy Water ($D_2O$):** Prepared by prolonged electrolysis of ordinary water (light water depletes faster, leaving D-enriched residue) or by the $H_2S$-process. Properties: mp = 3.8°C, bp = 101.4°C, density = 1.107 g/cm³. It slows neutrons effectively without absorbing them, making it an ideal moderator in nuclear reactors.

**Tritium ($^3_1H$):** A radioactive isotope that emits low-energy beta particles ($^3_1H \rightarrow ^3_2He + e^- + \bar{\nu}_e$). Used in self-luminous exit signs, as a tracer in environmental studies, and as fuel in hypothetical nuclear fusion reactors: $^2_1H + ^3_1H \rightarrow ^4_2He + n + 17.6\,\text{MeV}$.

**Hydrogen as Fuel — Combustion:** The combustion reaction $2H_2(g) + O_2(g) \rightarrow 2H_2O(l)$ releases $\Delta H = -572\,\text{kJ/mol}$ (286 kJ per mole of $H_2$). The calorific value is ~142 MJ/kg, about three times that of gasoline. The only emission is water vapour.

**Hydrogen Economy:** A proposed system where hydrogen is produced from renewable sources (green hydrogen via electrolysis), stored, transported, and used in fuel cells to generate electricity. Fuel cell reaction: $H_2 \rightarrow 2H^+ + 2e^-$ (anode), $\frac{1}{2}O_2 + 2H^+ + 2e^- \rightarrow H_2O$ (cathode).

**Storage Challenges:** Hydrogen's low volumetric energy density (0.0108 MJ/L at STP) makes storage difficult. Solutions include high-pressure cylinders (350–700 bar), liquefaction at 20 K (energy-intensive), and metal hydride storage (e.g., $LaNi_5H_6$). Leakage and embrittlement of metals are key engineering concerns.

**Nascent vs Atomic Hydrogen — Key Difference:** Nascent hydrogen is generated *during* a chemical reaction in solution and is highly reactive toward dissolved species. Atomic hydrogen is generated thermally or electrically in the gas phase at high temperature and is used for high-temperature welding. Both are monatomic but differ in generation method and application.

**Hydrogen Bond:** Though not an isotope concept, hydrogen bonding is crucial. When H is bonded to highly electronegative atoms (F, O, N), a partial positive charge on H attracts a lone pair on another electronegative atom. This explains the anomalously high boiling points of $H_2O$, $NH_3$, and $HF$.

**Perdeuterated Solvents in NMR:** Deuterated solvents (e.g., $CDCl_3$, $D_2O$) are used in proton NMR spectroscopy because deuterium does not produce signals in the ¹H frequency range. The deuterium signal is used for locking the spectrometer frequency. This is essential for structural elucidation of organic compounds.
confusion: ❌ Confusing nascent hydrogen with atomic hydrogen. ✅ Nascent hydrogen is generated in situ during a chemical reaction in solution (e.g., Zn + acid), while atomic hydrogen is produced by thermal or electrical dissociation of $H_2$ at high temperatures (~3000°C).

❌ Thinking heavy water ($D_2O$) is toxic to humans. ✅ $D_2O$ is not acutely toxic in small amounts, but prolonged consumption of large quantities replaces body water and disrupts cell division (mitosis) because the stronger D-bonds affect reaction kinetics — known as the kinetic isotope effect.

❌ Assuming tritium emits gamma radiation. ✅ Tritium undergoes pure beta decay ($\beta^-$) with a maximum energy of only 18.6 keV — it emits no gamma rays. This makes it relatively safe to handle with basic shielding (even glass stops the beta particles).

❌ Believing hydrogen can only act as a reducing agent. ✅ Hydrogen can also act as an oxidising agent when it reacts with active metals (e.g., $2Na + H_2 \rightarrow 2NaH$), accepting electrons to form the hydride ion $H^-$. Its role depends on the electronegativity of the reacting partner.

❌ Thinking $H_2$ and D₂ have identical chemical reaction rates. ✅ Due to the kinetic isotope effect, bonds involving deuterium are stronger (zero-point energy is lower), so reactions involving D₂ are generally slower. For example, the rate of $H_2 + Cl_2$ is faster than $D_2 + Cl_2$.

❌ Confusing the water-gas shift reaction with the water-gas reaction. ✅ The water-gas reaction is $C + H_2O \rightarrow CO + H_2$ (produces the syngas mixture). The water-gas *shift* reaction is $CO + H_2O \rightarrow CO_2 + H_2$ (converts CO to additional $H_2$ and removes CO). They are distinct steps in industrial hydrogen production.

❌ Assuming all hydrides are ionic. ✅ Hydrides are classified as ionic (saline, e.g., NaH), covalent (molecular, e.g., CH₄, H₂O), and metallic (interstitial, e.g., TiH₂). Transition metal hydrides are particularly important in catalysis and hydrogen storage.
practice:
**Problem 1:** Calculate the volume of hydrogen gas produced at STP when 6.5 g of zinc reacts completely with dilute $H_2SO_4$. ($Zn = 65\,\text{g/mol}$, molar volume at STP = 22.7 L/mol.)

**Solution:** Moles of Zn = $\frac{6.5}{65} = 0.1\,\text{mol}$. From $Zn + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow ZnSO_4 + H_2$, 1 mol Zn gives 1 mol $H_2$. Volume of $H_2$ = $0.1 \times 22.7 = 2.27\,\text{L}$. **Answer: 2.27 L.**

**Problem 2:** How much energy is released when 4 g of hydrogen is completely combusted? ($\Delta H_{comb} = -286\,\text{kJ/mol}$ for $H_2$.)

**Solution:** Moles of $H_2$ = $\frac{4}{2} = 2\,\text{mol}$. Energy released = $2 \times 286 = 572\,\text{kJ}$. **Answer: 572 kJ.**

**Problem 3:** A sample of water is found to contain 0.015% deuterium by atom. If 18 kg of this water is subjected to prolonged electrolysis, estimate the mass of $D_2O$ that can be obtained, assuming 100% enrichment efficiency.

**Solution:** 18 kg water = 1000 mol $H_2O$ = 2000 mol H atoms. Deuterium atoms = $0.00015 \times 2000 = 0.3\,\text{mol}$. Each $D_2O$ requires 2 D atoms, so moles of $D_2O$ = $\frac{0.3}{2} = 0.15\,\text{mol}$. Mass of $D_2O$ = $0.15 \times 20 = 3\,\text{g}$. **Answer: 3 g.**

**Problem 4:** In the nuclear fusion reaction $^2_1H + ^3_1H \rightarrow ^4_2He + n$, the masses are: $m(^2H) = 2.01410\,\text{u}$, $m(^3H) = 3.01605\,\text{u}$, $m(^4He) = 4.00260\,\text{u}$, $m(n) = 1.00866\,\text{u}$. Calculate the energy released per reaction in MeV. ($1\,\text{u} = 931.5\,\text{MeV}$.)

**Solution:** Mass defect $\Delta m = (2.01410 + 3.01605) - (4.00260 + 1.00866) = 5.03015 - 5.01126 = 0.01889\,\text{u}$. Energy = $0.01889 \times 931.5 = 17.59\,\text{MeV}$. **Answer: ≈ 17.6 MeV.**

**Problem 5:** Calculate the mass of $H_2$ that can be stored in 10 kg of the metal hydride $LaNi_5$ if it forms $LaNi_5H_6$.

**Solution:** Molar mass of $LaNi_5$ = 138.9 + 5(58.7) = 432.4 g/mol. Moles of $LaNi_5$ = $\frac{10000}{432.4} = 23.13\,\text{mol}$. Each mole absorbs 6 mol H₂, so moles of $H_2$ = $23.13 \times 6 = 138.8\,\text{mol}$. Mass of $H_2$ = $138.8 \times 2 = 277.6\,\text{g} \approx 0.278\,\text{kg}$. **Answer: 0.278 kg.**

**Problem 6:** The bond dissociation energy of $H_2$ is 436 kJ/mol. If 1 mol of $H_2$ is completely dissociated into atomic hydrogen, what is the wavelength of the photon required to break one H—H bond? ($h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{J·s}$, $c = 3 \times 10^8\,\text{m/s}$.)

**Solution:** Energy per bond = $\frac{436 \times 10^3}{6.022 \times 10^{23}} = 7.24 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$. Using $E = \frac{hc}{\lambda}$: $\lambda = \frac{6.626 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^8}{7.24 \times 10^{-19}} = 2.74 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{m} = 274\,\text{nm}$. **Answer: 274 nm (UV region).**
universalFacts: Hydrogen is the most abundant element in the universe, making up approximately 75% of all normal matter by mass. It powers stars through nuclear fusion, converting hydrogen into helium and releasing enormous energy.
Heavy water ($D_2O$) makes up about 1 atom of deuterium per 6420 atoms of hydrogen in natural water. Extracting 1 litre of pure $D_2O$ requires processing roughly 31 million litres of ordinary water.

The Hindenburg disaster (1937) is often cited as proof that hydrogen is dangerously flammable, but the real cause was the aluminized fabric skin — pure hydrogen burns with an invisible flame and was far less responsible for the catastrophe than commonly believed.

Liquid hydrogen has a temperature of 20.3 K (−252.9°C), making it one of the coldest substances encountered in everyday technology. It is used as rocket fuel in the Space Shuttle main engines and modern launch vehicles.

India has one of the world's most ambitious hydrogen programmes through the National Green Hydrogen Mission (2023), with a $2.3 billion allocation to make India a global hub for green hydrogen production and export by 2030.
